Text: Creating a `new File("path")` does not perform any {{c1::disk I/O}}; it only creates an abstract path representation in memory.
Extra: It is a common mistake to assume the constructor creates a physical file.

Text: File.createNewFile() returns {{c1::true}} if the file was successfully created, and {{c2::false}} if the file already exists.
Extra: It throws an IOException if parent directories do not exist.

Text: File.delete() will fail and return false if target is a directory that is {{c1::not empty}}.
Extra: To delete a directory containing files, you must recursively delete its children first.

Text: File.exists() checks for path presence, while File.isFile() and {{c1::File.isDirectory()}} check the node type.
Extra: Always check exists() first to avoid errors when reading properties.

Text: File.length() returns the file size in {{c1::bytes}}, and returns {{c2::0L}} if the file does not exist or is a directory.
Extra: This is an unbuffered metadata query.

Text: File.mkdir() fails if parent directories do not exist, whereas {{c1::File.mkdirs()}} creates all nonexistent parent directories recursively.
Extra: mkdirs() is much safer when writing nested project folders.

Text: InputStream is the abstract base class for reading {{c1::bytes}}, and its read() method returns {{c2::-1}} at the end of the stream.
Extra: read() blocks until a byte is available, EOF is reached, or an exception is thrown.

Text: OutputStream is the abstract base class for writing bytes, and must be closed to prevent {{c1::resource leaks}}.
Extra: Unclosed streams keep file handles open in the operating system.

Text: Wrapping resources in a {{c1::try-with-resources}} statement automatically closes them when exiting the block.
Extra: The class must implement AutoCloseable to be used in try-with-resources.

Text: FileOutputStream can write in append mode if the second constructor argument is set to {{c1::true}}.
Extra: For example, new FileOutputStream(file, true) appends bytes instead of truncating the file.

Text: BufferedInputStream stores bytes in an internal memory buffer of size {{c1::8KB}} by default to optimize OS system calls.
Extra: This minimizes disk access and improves I/O performance significantly.

Text: To write all buffered data from a BufferedOutputStream immediately to the output file, call the {{c1::flush()}} method.
Extra: Closing the stream also flushes data, but manual flushing is useful to ensure data is committed without closing.

Text: Reader and Writer character streams handle raw 16-bit Unicode characters and manage {{c1::character encoding}} translation automatically.
Extra: They translate bytes to chars using charset encoders and decoders.

Text: Using character streams to read or write binary files (like images) results in data {{c1::corruption}} due to character encoding mapping.
Extra: Encoding translates arbitrary binary byte values to replacement characters.

Text: Prior to Java 11, FileReader and FileWriter were bound to the default system {{c1::charset}}, rendering output platform-dependent.
Extra: Java 11 introduced constructors accepting a Charset parameter.

Text: BufferedReader reads text line-by-line using the {{c1::readLine()}} method, which returns {{c2::null}} when the end of stream is reached.
Extra: The returned string does not contain line termination characters.

Text: BufferedWriter provides the {{c1::newLine()}} method to write a platform-independent line separator.
Extra: This ensures files read correctly on Windows (\r\n) and Unix (\n).

Text: To serialize an object in Java, its class must implement the {{c1::Serializable}} marker interface.
Extra: Failing to do so throws a NotSerializableException.

Text: Attempting to serialize an object whose class does not implement Serializable throws {{c1::NotSerializableException}} at runtime.
Extra: All objects in the serialization graph must implement Serializable.

Text: During serialization, {{c1::static}} fields are not serialized because they represent class state, not instance state.
Extra: Static fields are resolved from class memory directly upon loading.

Text: Class fields marked with the {{c1::transient}} keyword are ignored during serialization and restored as {{c2::default}} values.
Extra: For example, reference fields restore as null, primitive ints as 0.

Text: Deserialization of an object does not run its own class constructor; instead, it runs the no-arg constructor of the first {{c1::non-serializable}} superclass.
Extra: This is a common interview trap regarding object instantiation cycles.

Text: A unique identifier named {{c1::serialVersionUID}} is verified during deserialization to ensure sender/receiver class compatibility.
Extra: If class definitions mismatch, deserialization fails.

Text: If a class changes after serialization and lacks an explicit serialVersionUID, deserialization throws {{c1::InvalidClassException}}.
Extra: Always declare serialVersionUID explicitly to avoid compiler changes throwing this error.

Text: Custom serialization can be achieved by declaring private {{c1::writeObject}} and {{c2::readObject}} methods inside the serializable class.
Extra: These methods allow encryption, decryption, or custom field state manipulation.

Text: Closing a Scanner wrapped around System.in will also close the underlying {{c1::System.in}} stream, making it impossible to read console input again.
Extra: Always avoid closing Scanner around System.in if you need standard input again in the application.

Text: System.in is an instance of InputStream, whereas System.out is an instance of {{c1::PrintStream}}.
Extra: PrintStream handles output formatting and does not throw IOException.

Text: System.err is typically {{c1::unbuffered}}, meaning output is immediately flushed to the console for error visibility.
Extra: In contrast, System.out is buffered by default.

Text: Deserializing a subclass fails if its non-serializable parent class does not possess a visible {{c1::no-argument constructor}}.
Extra: This throws an InvalidClassException at runtime.
